claim: Naked/NKD is a widely conserved feedback regulator of Wnt signaling which controls animal development and tissue homeostasis.
source: Naked/NKD is a widely conserved feedback regulator of Wnt signaling which controls animal development and tissue homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by the conservation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and cited literature.

claim: Naked/NKD destabilizes Dishevelled.
source: Naked/NKD destabilizes Dishevelled, which assembles Wnt signalosomes to inhibit the β-catenin destruction complex via recruitment of Axin.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1A and previous literature.

claim: The molecular mechanism underlying Naked/NKD function relies on its assembly into ultra-stable decameric core aggregates via its conserved C-terminal histidine cluster (HisC).
source: Here, we discover that the molecular mechanism underlying Naked/NKD function relies on its assembly into ultra-stable decameric core aggregates via its conserved C-terminal histidine cluster (HisC).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro data showing decameric core formation in Figure 2C and aggregation assays in Figure 2A,B.

claim: HisC aggregation is facilitated by Dishevelled.
source: HisC aggregation is facilitated by Dishevelled and depends on accumulation of Naked/NKD during prolonged Wnt stimulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in Figure 4C,D showing reduced HMW aggregates in DVL null cells.

claim: HisC aggregation depends on accumulation of Naked/NKD during prolonged Wnt stimulation.
source: HisC aggregation is facilitated by Dishevelled and depends on accumulation of Naked/NKD during prolonged Wnt stimulation.
evidence: This is shown by data in Figure 4A,B demonstrating concentration-dependent and Wnt-induced aggregation.

claim: Naked/NKD HisC cores co-aggregate with a conserved histidine cluster within Axin.
source: Naked/NKD HisC cores co-aggregate with a conserved histidine cluster within Axin, to destabilize it along with Dishevelled, possibly via the autophagy receptor p62, which binds to HisC aggregates.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro co-aggregation assays in Figure 3B and cellular coIP assays in Figure 1D.

claim: Naked/NKD co-aggregation with Axin destabilizes Axin along with Dishevelled.
source: Naked/NKD HisC cores co-aggregate with a conserved histidine cluster within Axin, to destabilize it along with Dishevelled, possibly via the autophagy receptor p62, which binds to HisC aggregates.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5B,C showing Axin1 and DVL2 destabilization.

claim: p62 autophagy receptor binds to HisC aggregates.
source: Naked/NKD HisC cores co-aggregate with a conserved histidine cluster within Axin, to destabilize it along with Dishevelled, possibly via the autophagy receptor p62, which binds to HisC aggregates.
evidence: This is demonstrated by BioID data in Figure 8B,C and coIP assays in Figure 8D.

claim: Attenuated Wnt responses are observed in CRISPR-engineered flies whose Naked/NKD HisC has been deleted.
source: Consistent with this, attenuated Wnt responses are observed in CRISPR-engineered flies and human epithelial cells whose Naked/NKD HisC has been deleted.
evidence: This is shown by cuticle phenotypes in Figure 6F and Figure 7C for Drosophila nkdΔhis mutants.

claim: Attenuated Wnt responses are observed in CRISPR-engineered human epithelial cells whose Naked/NKD HisC has been deleted.
source: Consistent with this, attenuated Wnt responses are observed in CRISPR-engineered flies and human epithelial cells whose Naked/NKD HisC has been deleted.
evidence: This is demonstrated by SuperTOP assays in Figure 5A showing reduced signaling in NKDΔHisC cells.

claim: HisC aggregation by Naked/NKD provides context-dependent feedback control of prolonged Wnt responses.
source: Thus, HisC aggregation by Naked/NKD provides context-dependent feedback control of prolonged Wnt responses.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing effects primarily during prolonged Wnt stimulation (Figure 5A,B).

claim: Dishevelled is a pivotal component within the ancient Wnt signaling pathway.
source: A well-studied hub protein is Dishevelled, a pivotal component within the ancient Wnt signaling pathway, which controls cell specification during development and adult tissue homeostasis throughout the animal kingdom (Cadigan and Nusse, 1997; Clevers et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on Dishevelled's role in Wnt signaling.

claim: Dishevelled transduces Wnt signals through canonical or non-canonical effector branches to elicit distinct cellular readouts.
source: Dishevelled transduces Wnt signals through canonical or non-canonical effector branches to elicit distinct cellular readouts, whereby the best-studied one is the β-catenin-dependent canonical branch which requires interaction of Dishevelled with Axin (Angers and Moon, 2009; Gammons and Bienz, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Dishevelled assembles signalosomes by dynamic head-to-tail polymerization of its DIX domain.
source: In order to transduce Wnt signals to β-catenin, Dishevelled assembles signalosomes by dynamic head-to-tail polymerization of its DIX domain (Schwarz-Romond et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on DIX domain polymerization.

claim: Dishevelled binds to the DIX domain of Axin, which leads to inhibition of the associated kinases in the β-catenin destruction complex.
source: This enables it to bind to the DIX domain of Axin, which leads to inhibition of the associated kinases in the β-catenin destruction complex Stamos et al., 2014 whose assembly, in the absence of signaling, depends on polymerization by the Axin DIX domain (Fiedler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on Dishevelled-Axin interaction and destruction complex inhibition.

claim: The flow through the canonical Wnt signaling pathway is determined by the opposing activities of polymerizing Axin and Dishevelled and their mutual interaction via their DIX domains.
source: In other words, the flow through the canonical Wnt signaling pathway is determined by the opposing activities of polymerizing Axin and Dishevelled and their mutual interaction via their DIX domains (Bienz, 2014)
evidence: This is a conceptual summary supported by the cited reference.

claim: The polymerization of Axin promotes destabilization of β-catenin and ensures quiescence of the pathway.
source: the polymerization of Axin promotes destabilization of β-catenin and therefore ensures quiescence of the pathway
evidence: This is established knowledge about Axin's role in the destruction complex.

claim: The polymerization of Dishevelled allows signalosome assembly and co-polymerization with Axin, which allows β-catenin to accumulate in the nucleus and engage in transcriptional activation of Wnt target genes.
source: while the polymerization of Dishevelled allows signalosome assembly and co-polymerization with Axin, which allows β-catenin to accumulate in the nucleus and engage in transcriptional activation of Wnt target genes (Gammons and Bienz, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on Dishevelled function in Wnt signaling.

claim: Recent high-resolution imaging studies have visualized endogenous Wnt signalosomes in mammalian cells, which result from limited polymerization of Dishevelled.
source: Recent high-resolution imaging studies have visualized endogenous Wnt signalosomes in mammalian cells, which result from limited polymerization of Dishevelled (Kan et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the cited imaging studies.

claim: Polymerization of Dishevelled and Axin is concentration-dependent.
source: Polymerization of Dishevelled and Axin is concentration-dependent (Schwarz-Romond et al., 2007), and occurs spontaneously if the cellular concentration of either of these proteins rises above a critical threshold.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on concentration-dependent polymerization.

claim: Spontaneous polymerization of Dishevelled or Axin above a critical threshold undermines the physiological control of the signaling flux by Wnt proteins, with detrimental consequences for cells including lethality.
source: This undermines the physiological control of the signaling flux by Wnt proteins, with detrimental consequences for cells including lethality (e.g. Fiedler et al., 2011; Penton et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references showing detrimental effects of uncontrolled polymerization.

claim: Dishevelled and Axin are each recognized by specific ubiquitin E3 ligases that allow their individual targeting for proteasomal degradation.
source: Indeed, Dishevelled and Axin are each recognized by specific ubiquitin E3 ligases that allow their individual targeting for proteasomal degradation (Angers et al., 2006; de Groot et al., 2014; Ji et al., 2017; Mund et al., 2015; Wei et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references on E3 ligase-mediated degradation.

claim: Dishevelled is targeted for degradation by autophagy via association with the autophagy receptor p62 and the ubiquitin-like proteins LC3 or GABARAPL.
source: In addition, Dishevelled is also targeted for degradation by autophagy via association with the autophagy receptor p62 and the ubiquitin-like proteins LC3 or GABARAPL (Gao et al., 2010; Ma et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on autophagy-mediated Dishevelled degradation.

claim: Naked was discovered in Drosophila as a Wnt-inducible antagonist of the Wnt pathway.
source: Naked was discovered in Drosophila as a Wnt-inducible antagonist of the Wnt pathway (Zeng et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on the original discovery of Naked.

claim: NKD orthologs accumulate upon Wnt stimulation of vertebrate cells.
source: NKD orthologs also accumulate upon Wnt stimulation of vertebrate cells, and Dishevelled was identified as a key target for downregulation by NKD (Rousset et al., 2001; Van Raay et al., 2007; Wharton et al., 2001; Yan et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on NKD accumulation and function.

claim: Dishevelled was identified as a key target for downregulation by NKD.
source: NKD orthologs also accumulate upon Wnt stimulation of vertebrate cells, and Dishevelled was identified as a key target for downregulation by NKD (Rousset et al., 2001; Van Raay et al., 2007; Wharton et al., 2001; Yan et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references identifying Dishevelled as an NKD target.

claim: Naked/NKD is the only known intracellular feedback regulator of Wnt signaling that is conserved throughout the animal kingdom.
source: Indeed, Naked/NKD is the only known intracellular feedback regulator of Wnt signaling that is conserved throughout the animal kingdom (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which argues strongly for its ubiquitous function and physiological relevance.
evidence: This is supported by the conservation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Naked/NKD function is not always essential.
source: However, Naked/NKD function is not always essential (e.g. mice can be born without Nkd proteins, albeit at submendelian ratios and with cranial bone abnormalities; Zhang et al., 2007), as is typical for modulatory feedback regulators, which are widespread and serve to canalize signal responses during development, and render them robust (Freeman, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on Nkd knockout mice and the concept of modulatory feedback regulators.

claim: Naked/NKD contains a single EF-hand, which binds to the PDZ domain of Dishevelled.
source: Molecularly, Naked/NKD contains a single EF-hand, which binds to the PDZ domain of Dishevelled (Rousset et al., 2001; Rousset et al., 2002; Wharton et al., 2001; Yan et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on the EF-hand-PDZ interaction and confirmed by SEC-MALS data in Figure 4E.

claim: The EF-hand of Naked/NKD binding to Dishevelled results in destabilization of Dishevelled, apparently via the ubiquitin/proteasome system.
source: This results in destabilization of Dishevelled, apparently via the ubiquitin/proteasome system (Guo et al., 2009; Hu et al., 2010; Schneider et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on Dishevelled destabilization.

claim: Cumulative evidence indicates that Naked/NKD affects both β-catenin-dependent and non-canonical Wnt signaling responses.
source: Cumulative evidence indicates that Naked/NKD affects both β-catenin-dependent and non-canonical Wnt signaling responses (Angonin and Van Raay, 2013; Creyghton et al., 2005; Hu et al., 2010; Marsden et al., 2018; Rousset et al., 2001; Schneider et al., 2010; Van Raay et al., 2007; Van Raay et al., 2007; Wharton et al., 2001; Yan et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references on Naked/NKD effects on different Wnt signaling branches.

claim: HA-Nkd1 reduces the signaling activity of co-overexpressed DVL2-GFP.
source: We used co-overexpression assays in HEK293T cells, monitoring Wnt signaling with a co-transfected β-catenin-dependent transcriptional reporter (SuperTOP) (Veeman et al., 2003), to confirm that murine HA-Nkd1 reduces the signaling activity of co-overexpressed DVL2-GFP (a human Dishevelled paralog), but not of co-overexpressed β-catenin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SuperTOP assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: HA-Nkd1 does not reduce the signaling activity of co-overexpressed β-catenin.
source: We used co-overexpression assays in HEK293T cells, monitoring Wnt signaling with a co-transfected β-catenin-dependent transcriptional reporter (SuperTOP) (Veeman et al., 2003), to confirm that murine HA-Nkd1 reduces the signaling activity of co-overexpressed DVL2-GFP (a human Dishevelled paralog), but not of co-overexpressed β-catenin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SuperTOP assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The downregulation of DVL2 signaling by Nkd1 depends on the EF-hand of Nkd1.
source: Previous work established that this downregulation depends on the EF-hand of Nkd1, the Dishevelled-binding domain (Rousset et al., 2001; Rousset et al., 2002; Wharton et al., 2001; Yan et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on the EF-hand requirement.

claim: HA-Nkd1 is less active in downregulating β-catenin signaling if its C-terminal HisC is deleted (ΔHisC).
source: In addition, HA-Nkd1 is also less active in downregulating β-catenin signaling if its C-terminal HisC is deleted (ΔHisC), despite the substantially higher expression levels of this deletion mutant (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SuperTOP assays and Western blots in Figure 1A.

claim: ΔHisC HA-Nkd1 has substantially higher expression levels than wild-type HA-Nkd1.
source: In addition, HA-Nkd1 is also less active in downregulating β-catenin signaling if its C-terminal HisC is deleted (ΔHisC), despite the substantially higher expression levels of this deletion mutant (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot in Figure 1A.

claim: HisC functions to destabilize Nkd1.
source: The latter is consistently observed, suggesting that HisC functions to destabilize Nkd1.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistently higher expression levels of ΔHisC mutants shown in Figure 1A and other figures.

claim: HA-Nkd1 coIPs with Flag-Axin1 upon co-expression.
source: Using co-immunoprecipitation (coIP) to monitor the association between co-expressed HA-Nkd1 and DVL2-GFP, we found that HA-Nkd1 also coIPs with Flag-Axin1 upon co-expression (Figure 1B), as previously observed (Miller et al., 2009).
evidence: This is demonstrated by coIP assays in Figure 1B and supported by a cited reference.

claim: HA-Nkd1, DVL2-GFP, and Flag-Axin1 can form a ternary complex.
source: This indicates that the three proteins can form a ternary complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the coIP data in Figure 1B showing all three proteins co-precipitating.

claim: Overexpressed Nkd1 forms high-molecular weight (HMW) aggregates that are resistant to boiling in sodium dodecyl sulphate (SDS).
source: While conducting these coIP assays, we discovered that overexpressed Nkd1 forms high-molecular weight (HMW) aggregates that are resistant to boiling in sodium dodecyl sulphate (SDS), and whose formation critically depends on HisC (Figure 1C
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blots in Figure 1C showing HMW bands.

claim: The formation of Nkd1 HMW aggregates critically depends on HisC.
source: While conducting these coIP assays, we discovered that overexpressed Nkd1 forms high-molecular weight (HMW) aggregates that are resistant to boiling in sodium dodecyl sulphate (SDS), and whose formation critically depends on HisC (Figure 1C
evidence: This is demonstrated by the absence of HMW bands in ΔHisC mutant in Figure 1C.

claim: Axin1-GFP specifically co-aggregates with HMW but not LMW (low-molecular weight) Flag-Nkd1 via its own internal HisC.
source: Notably, Axin1-GFP specifically co-aggregates with HMW but not LMW (low-molecular weight) Flag-Nkd1 via its own internal HisC (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by coIP assays in Figure 1D showing Axin1-GFP preferentially co-precipitating with HMW Nkd1.

claim: The simultaneous binding of Naked/NKD to Dishevelled and its co-aggregation with Axin may allow it to target Axin-containing Wnt signalosomes.
source: Thus, our data are consistent with the notion that the simultaneous binding of Naked/NKD to Dishevelled and its co-aggregation with Axin may allow it to target Axin-containing Wnt signalosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the ternary complex formation and co-aggregation data in Figure 1B,D.

claim: Recombinant Lip-NKD-HisC forms stable aggregates that elute as a broad peak in the 250–450 kDa range (corresponding to 15–25-mers) by size exclusion chromatography (SEC).
source: Indeed, Lip-NKD-HisC forms stable aggregates that elute as a broad peak in the 250–450 kDa range (corresponding to 15–25-mers), as monitored by size exclusion chromatography (SEC) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC data in Figure 2A.

claim: If the pH is lowered below ~ 6.5, Lip-NKD-HisC aggregates begin to dissociate.
source: If the pH is lowered below ~ 6.5, these aggregates begin to dissociate, and Lip-NKD-HisC is completely monomeric at pH 5 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC and PAGE data in Figure 2A,B showing pH-dependent dissociation.

claim: Lip-NKD-HisC is completely monomeric at pH 5.
source: If the pH is lowered below ~ 6.5, these aggregates begin to dissociate, and Lip-NKD-HisC is completely monomeric at pH 5 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC and PAGE data in Figure 2B.

claim: The sharp pH-dependence of NKD-HisC aggregation reflects the pKa value (~6.0) of the imidazole side-chain of His.
source: This sharp pH-dependence reflects the pKa value (~6.0) of the imidazole side-chain of His: in acidic conditions (pH < 6), this side-chain is protonated and positively charged, and aggregation is thus blocked by electrostatic repulsion, whereas at higher pH values (pH > 6.2), the majority of His side-chains are uncharged, which is permissive for NKD-HisC core formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the pH-dependent aggregation data in Figure 2A,B and knowledge of histidine chemistry.

claim: An ultra-stable NKD-HisC core of ~ 150 kDa is observed by PAGE under denaturing and reducing conditions.
source: If assayed by polyacryl-amide gel electrophoresis (PAGE) under denaturating and reducing conditions (i.e. after boiling in 1% w/v SDS and 5% v/v mercapto-ethanol), an ultra-stable NKD-HisC core of ~ 150 kDa is observed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by PAGE data in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The stable NKD-HisC core consists of a 10-mer.
source: This core was sized more accurately by mixing monomeric Lip-NKD-HisC with monomeric NKD-HisC bearing a Maltose-Binding Protein tag (MBP-NKD-HisC) at different ratios at acidic pH, and by increasing the pH subsequently, to allow aggregation. Because of the different molecular masses of these tags, we observe a discrete laddering on PAGE, revealing that the stable NKD-HisC core consists of a 10-mer (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the laddering pattern in co-aggregation assays in Figure 2C.

claim: The formation of NKD-HisC aggregates depends on the most conserved histidines.
source: Notably, the formation of NKD-HisC aggregates not only depends on the most conserved histidines, but also on two aromatic residues within HisC that are highly conserved amongst Naked/NKD orthologs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1): double- or quintuple point-substitutions of the most conserved histidine or aromatic residues (m1-m3) strongly reduce aggregation of recombinant Lip-NKD-HisC (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mutational analysis in Figure 2D.

claim: The formation of NKD-HisC aggregates depends on two aromatic residues within HisC that are highly conserved amongst Naked/NKD orthologs.
source: Notably, the formation of NKD-HisC aggregates not only depends on the most conserved histidines, but also on two aromatic residues within HisC that are highly conserved amongst Naked/NKD orthologs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1): double- or quintuple point-substitutions of the most conserved histidine or aromatic residues (m1-m3) strongly reduce aggregation of recombinant Lip-NKD-HisC (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mutational analysis in Figure 2D and conservation analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: NKD-HisC aggregates into a decameric ultra-stable core that can be decorated by additional NKD-HisC monomers that are less firmly associated.
source: Our results indicate that NKD-HisC aggregates into a decameric ultra-stable core (called HisC core below) that can be decorated by additional NKD-HisC monomers that are less firmly associated (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is inferred from the SEC and co-aggregation data in Figure 2A,C showing both stable cores and larger aggregates.

claim: The two double-point mutations (m1, m2) attenuate aggregation of HA-Nkd1 in cells.
source: Indeed, the two double-point mutations (m1, m2) attenuate aggregation of HA-Nkd1 in cells, particularly noticeable when co-expressed with Flag-DVL2, while the quintuple mutation (m3) is almost as strong as ΔHisC in blocking aggregation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blots in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The quintuple mutation (m3) is almost as strong as ΔHisC in blocking aggregation of HA-Nkd1 in cells.
source: Indeed, the two double-point mutations (m1, m2) attenuate aggregation of HA-Nkd1 in cells, particularly noticeable when co-expressed with Flag-DVL2, while the quintuple mutation (m3) is almost as strong as ΔHisC in blocking aggregation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blots in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Each of the three HisC mutations (m1, m2, m3) stabilizes HA-Nkd1.
source: Notably, each of the three mutations also stabilizes HA-Nkd1, with m3 being almost as potent as ΔHisC.
evidence: This is shown by increased protein levels of mutants in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Despite their significantly increased levels, none of the three HisC mutants (m1, m2, m3) is as active as wt HA-Nkd1 in antagonizing Flag-DVL2 signaling.
source: However, despite their significantly increased levels, none of the three mutants is as active as wt HA-Nkd1 in antagonizing Flag-DVL2 signaling: m1 reduces signaling only partially, while m2 and m3 abolish the activity of HA-Nkd1 in antagonizing Flag-DVL2 signaling (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SuperTOP assays in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The HisC-dependent aggregation observed in vitro is required for the activity of Nkd1 in antagonizing DVL2 signaling in cells.
source: They provide strong evidence that the HisC-dependent aggregation observed in vitro is required for the activity of Nkd1 in antagonizing DVL2 signaling in cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between reduced aggregation and reduced activity of HisC mutants shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A search of the human genome for proteins exhibiting a minimum of eight His residues within a 13 amino acid stretch identified 74 proteins (containing 78 HisC sequences).
source: We searched the human genome for proteins exhibiting a minimum of eight His residues within a 13 amino acid stretch, which identified 74 proteins (containing 78 HisC sequences; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on a bioinformatic search of the human genome.

claim: Most HisC-containing proteins in the human genome are nuclear proteins and thus unlikely targets for Naked/NKD.
source: Most of these are nuclear proteins and thus unlikely targets for Naked/NKD, which is anchored at the plasma membrane by its N-terminus via myristoylation (Chan et al., 2007; Hu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the subcellular localization of HisC-containing proteins and cited references on NKD myristoylation.

claim: The non-nuclear set of HisC-containing proteins contains Axin1 and Prickle3.
source: The non-nuclear set contains Axin1 and Prickle3 (a non-canonical Wnt signaling component) as well as a small number of additional proteins (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in the table in Figure 3A.

claim: MBP-Axin1-HisC exhibits the most pronounced co-aggregation with Lip-NKD-HisC (<5 molecules per core, at equivalent ratio).
source: We tested a subset of these HisC (tagged with MBP) for in vitro co-aggregation, and found that MBP-Axin1-HisC exhibits the most pronounced co-aggregation with Lip-NKD-HisC (<5 molecules per core, at equivalent ratio; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-aggregation assays in Figure 3B.

claim: Axin2 exhibits an internal HisC, which co-aggregates with Lip-NKD-HisC (<4 molecules per core, at equivalent ratio).
source: Axin2 also exhibits an internal HisC, which co-aggregates with Lip-NKD-HisC (<4 molecules per core, at equivalent ratio), although this seems insufficient for its co-aggregation with ultra-stable Nkd1 HisC cores in cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-aggregation assays in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The MBP-HisCs from the remaining tested HisC-containing proteins co-aggregate poorly, or not at all, with Lip-NKD-HisC.
source: The MBP-HisCs from the remaining tested HisC-containing proteins co-aggregate poorly, or not at all, with Lip-NKD-HisC (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-aggregation assays in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Axin1 is likely the primary if not only physiological target for NKD co-aggregation within the human genome.
source: Given the sequence conservation of the HisC in Axin orthologs, the specificity and avidity of co-aggregation between Axin1-HisC and NKD1 HisC cores in vitro and the co-aggregation between Axin1 and Nkd1 in cells, it seems likely that Axin1 is the primary if not only physiological target for NKD co-aggregation within the human genome.
evidence: This is inferred from the specificity of co-aggregation shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2, and cellular co-aggregation in Figure 1D.

claim: The level of SDS-resistant HMW Nkd1 aggregates depends on the level of Nkd1 overexpression.
source: The level of SDS-resistant HMW Nkd1 aggregates clearly depends on the level of Nkd1 overexpression, indicating that HisC aggregation is concentration-dependent (Figure 4A
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blots in Figure 4A showing increasing HMW aggregates with increasing Nkd1 expression.

claim: HisC aggregation is concentration-dependent.
source: The level of SDS-resistant HMW Nkd1 aggregates clearly depends on the level of Nkd1 overexpression, indicating that HisC aggregation is concentration-dependent (Figure 4A
evidence: This is inferred from the dose-dependent increase in HMW aggregates shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Wnt stimulation promotes Nkd1 aggregation.
source: We therefore asked whether Wnt stimulation (which increases Nkd1 expression; Van Raay et al., 2007; Yan et al., 2001) would promote Nkd1 aggregation, which is indeed the case (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blots in Figure 4B showing increased HMW aggregates with Wnt stimulation.

claim: Dishevelled stimulates efficient Nkd1 aggregation since the formation of HMW aggregates is much reduced in DVL null cells.
source: In addition, Dishevelled stimulates efficient Nkd1 aggregation since the formation of HMW aggregates is much reduced in DVL null cells (lacking all three DVL paralog; Gammons et al., 2016b; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blots in Figure 4C showing reduced HMW aggregates in DVL null cells.

claim: Polymerization-deficient DVL2 mutants or DVL2 lacking its DIX domain are most active in restoring formation of Nkd1 HMW aggregates upon re-expression in DVL null cells.
source: We thus found that polymerization-deficient mutants or DVL2 lacking its DIX domain were most active, while DVL2 mutants whose DEP-dependent dimerization is blocked (E499G or G436P) were least active (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blots in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: DVL2 mutants whose DEP-dependent dimerization is blocked (E499G or G436P) are least active in restoring formation of Nkd1 HMW aggregates upon re-expression in DVL null cells.
source: We thus found that polymerization-deficient mutants or DVL2 lacking its DIX domain were most active, while DVL2 mutants whose DEP-dependent dimerization is blocked (E499G or G436P) were least active (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blots in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The formation of stable DVL2 dimers formed by DEP domain swapping is crucial for Nkd1 aggregation.
source: This indicates that the formation of stable DVL2 dimers formed by DEP domain swapping is crucial for Nkd1 aggregation.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for DEP-dependent dimerization shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Restoration of Nkd1 HMW aggregates depends on the PDZ domain of DVL2.
source: As expected, restoration of HMW aggregates also depends on the PDZ domain, the NKD-binding domain of DVL2 (Rousset et al., 2001; Wharton et al., 2001; Yan et al., 2001), but is hardly affected by K446M, which blocks binding of the DEP domain to the Frizzled receptor (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blots in Figure 4D and supported by cited references.

claim: A stable complex forms between the DVL2 PDZ domain and the Nkd1 EF-hand.
source: To confirm that the DVL2 PDZ domain binds directly to the Nkd1 EF-hand, we used SEC followed by multi-angle light scattering (SEC-MALS) of purified recombinant domains to show that a stable complex forms between them (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC-MALS data in Figure 4E.

claim: The binding affinity between the DVL2 PDZ domain and the Nkd1 EF-hand is in the low-micromolar range (Kd 3.2 ± 0.2 μM).
source: Using isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC), we estimated a binding affinity in the low-micromolar range (Kd3.2 ± 0.2 μM), which depends on the integrity of the PDZ cleft as demonstrated by the failure of the EF-hand to bind to the V334E cleft mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) whose binding to cognate substrate motifs is abolished (Gammons et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ITC data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The binding between the DVL2 PDZ domain and the Nkd1 EF-hand depends on the integrity of the PDZ cleft.
source: Using isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC), we estimated a binding affinity in the low-micromolar range (Kd3.2 ± 0.2 μM), which depends on the integrity of the PDZ cleft as demonstrated by the failure of the EF-hand to bind to the V334E cleft mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) whose binding to cognate substrate motifs is abolished (Gammons et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ITC data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing no binding to V334E mutant.

claim: The molecular mass of the EF-hand-PDZ complex indicates that the PDZ domain binds to an EF-hand dimer.
source: Interestingly, the molecular mass of the EF-hand-PDZ complex indicates that the PDZ domain binds to an EF-hand dimer (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is inferred from the SEC-MALS data in Figure 4E showing a complex mass consistent with 2 EF-hands and 1 PDZ domain.

claim: A single DVL2 dimer can bind to four molecules of Nkd1.
source: Taken together with our previous results (Figure 4D), this implies that a single DVL2 dimer can bind to four molecules of Nkd1, resulting in a considerable increase of its local concentration, which may provide the trigger for the formation of HisC core aggregates.
evidence: This is inferred from the DEP dimer requirement (Figure 4D) and the 2:1 EF-hand:PDZ stoichiometry (Figure 4E).

claim: NKD null cells show a normal response to Wnt3a during the first ~ 3 hrs.
source: Somewhat to our surprise, NKD null cells show a normal response to Wnt3a during the first ~ 3 hr (hrs) (Figure 5A,B), with no detectable hyperactivation of β-catenin-dependent transcription.
evidence: This is demonstrated by SuperTOP assays and Western blots in Figure 5A,B.

claim: By ~ 6 hr of Wnt3a stimulation, the signaling response of NKD null cells is noticeably attenuated and begins to plateau.
source: However, by ~ 6 hr of Wnt3a stimulation, their signaling response is noticeably attenuated and begins to plateau, unlike the response of parental control cells which continues to rise, reaching at least three times the levels compared to that of the NKD null cells by 12 hr (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SuperTOP assays in Figure 5A.

claim: The Wnt response is significantly reduced from 6 hr onwards in NKDΔHisC lines.
source: Similarly, the Wnt response is also significantly reduced from 6 hr onwards in two independently isolated NKDΔHisC lines, although this reduction is less pronounced than in NKD null cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SuperTOP assays in Figure 5A.

claim: NKD functions as a positive regulator of Wnt signaling in human epithelial cells.
source: These results provide clear evidence that NKD functions as a positive regulator of Wnt signaling in these human epithelial cells, and reveal the functional importance of its histidine cluster in the maintenance of Wnt responses during prolonged Wnt stimulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced Wnt signaling in NKD null and NKDΔHisC cells shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The histidine cluster of NKD is functionally important in the maintenance of Wnt responses during prolonged Wnt stimulation.
source: These results provide clear evidence that NKD functions as a positive regulator of Wnt signaling in these human epithelial cells, and reveal the functional importance of its histidine cluster in the maintenance of Wnt responses during prolonged Wnt stimulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the reduced signaling in NKDΔHisC cells shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The levels of endogenous Axin1 gradually decrease to approximately half within the first 6 hr after Wnt stimulation in parental HEK293T cells.
source: Indeed, while the levels of endogenous Axin1 gradually decrease to approximately half within the first 6 hr after Wnt stimulation in parental HEK293T cells, they decrease less in NKDΔHisC cells (Figure 5B), and there is no statistically significant reduction of the Axin1 levels in NKD null cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blots and densitometry in Figure 5B.

claim: The levels of endogenous Axin1 decrease less in NKDΔHisC cells compared to parental cells after Wnt stimulation.
source: Indeed, while the levels of endogenous Axin1 gradually decrease to approximately half within the first 6 hr after Wnt stimulation in parental HEK293T cells, they decrease less in NKDΔHisC cells (Figure 5B), and there is no statistically significant reduction of the Axin1 levels in NKD null cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blots and densitometry in Figure 5B.

claim: There is no statistically significant reduction of the Axin1 levels in NKD null cells after Wnt stimulation.
source: Indeed, while the levels of endogenous Axin1 gradually decrease to approximately half within the first 6 hr after Wnt stimulation in parental HEK293T cells, they decrease less in NKDΔHisC cells (Figure 5B), and there is no statistically significant reduction of the Axin1 levels in NKD null cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blots and densitometry in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The levels of endogenous DVL2 are elevated in NKDΔHisC cells.
source: Similarly, the levels of endogenous DVL2 are elevated in NKDΔHisC (Figure 5B) and NKD null cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), most noticeable for the Wnt-induced phosphorylated form.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blots in Figure 5B.

claim: The levels of endogenous DVL2 are elevated in NKD null cells.
source: Similarly, the levels of endogenous DVL2 are elevated in NKDΔHisC (Figure 5B) and NKD null cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), most noticeable for the Wnt-induced phosphorylated form.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blots in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Axin1 and DVL2 are both stabilized during prolonged Wnt stimulation in cells without functional NKD.
source: Thus, Axin1 and DVL2 are both stabilized during prolonged Wnt stimulation in cells without functional NKD, indicating that NKD functions to target both signalosome components for degradation in these cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the elevated levels of Axin1 and DVL2 in NKD-deficient cells shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: NKD functions to target both Axin1 and DVL2 signalosome components for degradation.
source: Thus, Axin1 and DVL2 are both stabilized during prolonged Wnt stimulation in cells without functional NKD, indicating that NKD functions to target both signalosome components for degradation in these cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the stabilization of both proteins in NKD-deficient cells shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Axin1 rather than DVL2 is rate-limiting for a sustained Wnt response of HEK293T cells.
source: Its requirement for maintaining β-catenin responses can readily be explained by its destabilizing effect on Axin1 but not on DVL2 (see also Discussion), which argues that Axin1 rather than DVL2 is rate-limiting for a sustained Wnt response of these cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between Axin1 stabilization and reduced β-catenin signaling in NKD-deficient cells shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Overexpressed Nkd1 but not Nkd1ΔHisC accelerates the destabilization of endogenous Axin1 upon Wnt stimulation.
source: Indeed, overexpressed Nkd1 but not Nkd1ΔHisC (incapable of forming HMW aggregates) accelerates the destabilization of endogenous Axin1 upon Wnt stimulation, but does not affect the levels of endogenous DVL2 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blots in Figure 5C.

claim: Overexpressed Nkd1 does not affect the levels of endogenous DVL2 upon Wnt stimulation.
source: Indeed, overexpressed Nkd1 but not Nkd1ΔHisC (incapable of forming HMW aggregates) accelerates the destabilization of endogenous Axin1 upon Wnt stimulation, but does not affect the levels of endogenous DVL2 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blots in Figure 5C.

claim: Homozygous nkd13 embryos exhibit stretches of excess naked cuticle.
source: As expected, homozygous nkd13 embryos exhibit stretches of excess naked cuticle, however, these mutant embryos also show near-normal denticle belts that are uninterrupted by naked patches (Figure 6E), more so than the mutant embryos bearing h1 (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cuticle images in Figure 6E.

claim: Patches of missing denticles in nkd13 embryos are predominantly observed in rows 3–7.
source: Notably, patches of missing denticles in nkd13 embryos are predominantly observed in rows 3–7 (Figure 7B), and seem to correlate with the sporadic patches of ectopic Wg expression (Martinez Arias et al., 1988; Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is demonstrated by denticle quantification in Figure 7B and Wg staining in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: nkd13 and nkdΔhis homozygous embryos exhibit excess row-0 denticles.
source: On close examination of the near-normal denticle belts in nkd13 embryos, we noticed ectopic small denticles anteriorly to these belts (Figure 7C), i.e. in row 0 (Figure 7A). This phenotype, observed in ~ 20% of near-normal denticle belts of nkd13 homozygotes (Figure 7C), signifies a reduced Wg response in this part of the segment.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cuticle images and quantification in Figure 7C.

claim: Excess row-0 denticles in nkd mutants signify a reduced Wg response.
source: This phenotype, observed in ~ 20% of near-normal denticle belts of nkd13 homozygotes (Figure 7C), signifies a reduced Wg response in this part of the segment.
evidence: This is inferred from knowledge of denticle specification by Wg signaling.

claim: The expression of UbxB.lacZ is reduced consistently in nkd13 mutant embryos.
source: We also examined the expression of a Wg-responsive reporter from the Ultrabithorax gene (UbxB.lacZ) (Thüringer et al., 1993) as a direct readout of Wg signaling in the middle midgut of late-stage embryos (Riese et al., 1997), and found this to be reduced consistently in nkd13 mutant embryos (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by antibody staining in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Naked functions in late embryonic stages to maintain Wg signaling responses.
source: This further underscores the notion that Naked functions in late embryonic stages to maintain Wg signaling responses.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced UbxB.lacZ expression and excess row-0 denticles in nkd mutants shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Homozygous nkdΔhis flies can be obtained, however ~ 20% of their offspring die as late-stage embryos.
source: Homozygous nkd Δhis flies can be obtained, however ~ 20% of their offspring die as late-stage embryos.
evidence: This is based on observations of nkdΔhis fly viability.

claim: Each nkdΔhis late-stage lethal embryo shows several abnormal denticle belts with disordered denticle rows, misoriented denticles as well as excess small denticles in their anterior regions.
source: Each of these embryos shows several abnormal denticle belts with disordered denticle rows, misoriented denticles as well as excess small denticles in their anterior regions (Figure 6F and 7C)
evidence: This is demonstrated by cuticle images in Figure 6F and Figure 7C.

claim: The excess anterior denticles in nkdΔhis mutant embryos parallel the Wnt signaling defect of the NKDΔHis human cells.
source: It thus appears that these excess anterior denticles in nkd Δhis mutant embryos parallels the Wnt signaling defect of the NKDΔHis human cells (Figure 5A), implicating the C-terminal HisC of Drosophila Naked in the maintenance of the Wg response throughout late embryonic stages.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity between fly and human phenotypes shown in Figure 5A and Figure 7C.

claim: The C-terminal HisC of Drosophila Naked is implicated in the maintenance of the Wg response throughout late embryonic stages.
source: It thus appears that these excess anterior denticles in nkd Δhis mutant embryos parallels the Wnt signaling defect of the NKDΔHis human cells (Figure 5A), implicating the C-terminal HisC of Drosophila Naked in the maintenance of the Wg response throughout late embryonic stages.
evidence: This is inferred from the nkdΔhis phenotype shown in Figure 6F and Figure 7C.

claim: p62 and NBR1 are the top HisC-dependent hits from BioID proximity labeling.
source: Strikingly, our top HisC-dependent hits are the two main autophagy receptors p62 and NBR1 (Kirkin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BioID data in Figure 8B.

claim: Nkd1-BirA* binds to endogenous p62 in a HisC-dependent fashion.
source: We used BioID proximity-labeling (BioIP) to confirm that Nkd1-BirA* binds to endogenous p62 in a HisC-dependent fashion (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BioIP assays in Figure 8C.

claim: The association between Nkd1 and p62 is independent of Dishevelled.
source: However, the association between Nkd1 and p62 is independent of Dishevelled since the two proteins coIP as efficiently in DVL null cells as in control HEK293T cells (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by coIP assays in Figure 8D.

claim: The p62-interacting domain of Nkd1 is its EF-hand.
source: We used internal deletions to map the p62-interacting domain of Nkd1 to its EF-hand (Figure 8D)
evidence: This is demonstrated by coIP assays with deletion mutants in Figure 8D.

claim: Co-expressed Flag-p62 shows a strong preference for binding to HMW HA-Nkd1.
source: As expected from our BioID screen, co-expressed Flag-p62 shows a strong preference for binding to HMW HA-Nkd1 (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by coIP assays in Figure 8D.

claim: p62 may bind to Nkd1 HisC aggregates and Nkd1-Axin1 co-aggregates, to target these for autophagy-dependent degradation.
source: These results suggest that p62 may bind to Nkd1 HisC aggregates and Nkd1-Axin1 co-aggregates, to target these for autophagy-dependent degradation (see Discussion).
evidence: This is inferred from the p62 binding data in Figure 8C,D and knowledge of p62's role in autophagy.

claim: Both negative and positive regulatory effects of Naked/NKD on Wnt signaling are mediated by its activity to destabilize its interaction partners.
source: Both negative and positive regulatory effects of Naked/NKD on Wnt signaling are mediated by its activity to destabilize its interaction partners.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing destabilization of both Dishevelled and Axin in Figure 5B,C.

claim: Whether Naked/NKD antagonizes or promotes Wnt signaling appears to depend on whether Dishevelled or Axin is limiting for Wnt responses in any given cell.
source: Therefore, whether Naked/NKD antagonizes or promotes Wnt signaling appears to depend on whether Dishevelled or Axin is limiting for Wnt responses in any given cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the context-dependent effects of NKD on Wnt signaling shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: NKD-HisC core aggregates are decameric.
source: NKD-HisC core aggregates are decameric, and their finite size implies a well-defined structure.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-aggregation assays in Figure 2C.

claim: The finite size of NKD-HisC core aggregates implies a well-defined structure.
source: NKD-HisC core aggregates are decameric, and their finite size implies a well-defined structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the discrete decameric size shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Because of their oligomeric nature, Naked/NKD-HisC aggregates attain a high avidity for Axin-HisC.
source: Because of their oligomeric nature, Naked/NKD-HisC aggregates attain a high avidity for Axin-HisC, enabling these two proteins to interact efficiently.
evidence: This is inferred from the decameric structure and specific co-aggregation shown in Figure 2C and Figure 3B.

claim: The physiological relevance of the HisC-dependent aggregation of Naked/NKD is indicated by specific HisC deletions in human cells.
source: The physiological relevance of the HisC-dependent aggregation of Naked/NKD is indicated by specific HisC deletions in human cells: their signaling defects following prolonged Wnt stimulation (reduced β-catenin responses, and stabilization of Axin; Figure 5A,B; Figure 5—figure supplement 2) are consistent with precocious termination of Wnt signaling by Axin
evidence: This is demonstrated by the phenotypes of NKDΔHisC cells shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Naked/NKD acts similarly to the ubiquitin E3 ligase SIAH which targets Axin for proteasomal degradation upon Wnt signaling.
source: It therefore seems that Naked/NKD acts similarly to the ubiquitin E3 ligase SIAH which targets Axin for proteasomal degradation upon Wnt signaling (Ji et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the similar effects on Axin stability and supported by the cited reference.

claim: Naked/NKD and SIAH may function redundantly to destabilize Axin.
source: Indeed, the two factors may function redundantly to destabilize Axin, thereby maintaining Wnt signaling responses by preventing Axin from re-establishing quiescence too early.
evidence: This is speculated based on their similar effects on Axin.

claim: The marked concentration-dependence of HisC core aggregation ensures that Naked/NKD only aggregates once it has accumulated upon prolonged Wnt signaling.
source: The marked concentration-dependence of HisC core aggregation (Figure 4A) ensures that Naked/NKD only aggregates once it has accumulated upon prolonged Wnt signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the concentration-dependent aggregation shown in Figure 4A.

claim: DEP-dependent dimerization of Dishevelled is a prerequisite for facilitating Naked/NKD aggregation.
source: Furthermore, aggregation is promoted by Dishevelled, and our evidence indicates that DEP-dependent dimerization of Dishevelled is a prerequisite for facilitating Naked/NKD aggregation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the requirement for DEP dimerization shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The interaction between Dishevelled and Naked/NKD results in a considerable increase (>4 fold) in local concentration of Naked/NKD.
source: Since the PDZ domain of Dishevelled binds to a dimer of NKD EF-hands, this implies that the interaction between the two proteins results in a considerable increase (>4 fold) in local concentration of Naked/NKD, which may overcome the threshold necessary for triggering HisC aggregation.
evidence: This is inferred from the stoichiometry data in Figure 4E and the DEP dimer requirement in Figure 4D.

claim: The dual dependence of Naked/NKD aggregation on Wnt stimulation and Dishevelled dimerization could safeguard against fortuitous spontaneous aggregation.
source: The dual dependence of Naked/NKD aggregation on Wnt stimulation and Dishevelled dimerization could safeguard against fortuitous spontaneous aggregation and, thus, inappropriate destabilization of Axin.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirements for both Wnt stimulation (Figure 4B) and Dishevelled (Figure 4C,D).

claim: Dishevelled and Naked/NKD may remain associated following HisC aggregation.
source: Given the moderately stable interaction between Dishevelled and Naked/NKD (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), it seems plausible that the two proteins remain associated following HisC aggregation, which could lead to the destabilization of Dishevelled alongside Axin.
evidence: This is speculated based on the binding affinity data.

claim: The stabilization of DVL2 in NKDΔHisC cells during prolonged Wnt stimulation may explain why loss-of-function of Naked/NKD can lead to hyperactive Wnt signaling.
source: In support of this is the stabilization of DVL2 in NKDΔHisC cells during prolonged Wnt stimulation (Figure 5B), which may explain why loss-of-function of Naked/NKD can lead to hyperactive Wnt signaling, and interfere with PCP signaling (Hu et al., 2010; Marsden et al., 2018; Rousset et al., 2001; Schneider et al., 2010; Van Raay et al., 2007; Zeng et al., 2000).
evidence: This is inferred from the DVL2 stabilization data in Figure 5B and cited references.

claim: The destabilization of Naked/NKD-binding partners is mediated by autophagy.
source: Our discovery of the p62 and NBR1 autophagy receptors as Nkd1-interacting proteins suggests that the destabilization of Naked/NKD-binding partners is mediated by autophagy.
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of p62 and NBR1 as binding partners in Figure 8B,C.

claim: The targeting of NKD-binding partners to autophagosomes is contingent on Naked/NKD aggregation.
source: This binding preference implies that the targeting of NKD-binding partners to autophagosomes is contingent on Naked/NKD aggregation.
evidence: This is inferred from the preferential binding of p62 to HMW Nkd1 shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Naked/NKD-HisC cores act as adaptors between Wnt signalosomes and autophagy receptors.
source: Indeed, there appears to be an interaction network between Dishevelled, p62, Axin and aggregated Naked/NKD, implicating Naked/NKD-HisC cores as adaptors between Wnt signalosomes and autophagy receptors, as an alternative route to the SIAH pathway (Ji et al., 2017) for the disposal of Axin and other signalosome components upon Wnt signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the interaction data in Figure 8B,C,D.
